chapter: The craft of the ad lib player
title: Recording with Louis Jordan's Tympany Five for Decca
summary: Hall became Decca's house bass player after Jordan's first dates and recalls tunes and Jordan's earlier career.

bands.name: Louis Jordan and His Tympany Five

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Well, then that becomes an ego thing. I remember working the first dates bass with Louis Jordan's band. The original Timpany Five, He didn't have a bass player on (inaudible) just for records, and I was chosen for Decca. And the engineers at Decca said I had the most perfect beat of all the rest of the bass players, so I became the house bass player there with all the

blues singers
bass players and whatnot.
Do you remember what records you made with Louis Jordan (inaudible)?
Doug the Jitterbug was one.
I have that record.
And --
"Flatface" --
"Keep A-knockin' But You Can't Come In."
I have that.
And -- oh, gee, I don't remember all of them.
Yeah, but they were some of the early ones.
They were the first ones, the first recordings of his group.
Yeah, I remember we had "Doug the Jitterbug" and "Flatface" was the other side. My brother had that record. It was one of my favorites. Did you also make "Sam Jones Done Snagged His Britches?"
Yes, I made that too.
Those have never been reissued either. I'd love to get Milt Gabler, whoever was over there --
I have the originals of that.
-- to reissue those on LP, because
they put out mostly his biggest hits. Everything should be out on Louis Jordan.

Right. Right. He's a very energetic musician. He knows how to handle the bandstand and how to get the most out of what he had to do. I worked with Louis Jordan when I was in Philadelphia and first started playing bass, when he was the saxophone player with Charlie Gainsecks, orchestra and then he --
Then he was with Chick Webb later on.
Then he came to New York with Chick Webb, yes. And after Chick Webb, then he went out on his own.
Now, it's called the Tympani Five.
Tympani Five, but they were six.
But there was no Tympani in person, but on the records they used -- did they use tympani?
That was the -- no, no.
It was just the --
No.
Because sometimes there are some effects that almost sound like —
(inaudible).
I can't recall ever -- I can't recall a tympani being used on any of the dates.
